lead: Spread spectrum takes a narrowband signal and spreads it over a much wider band using a code known to the receiver. Total power stays the same, so power per hertz falls and the signal can sit below the noise floor. Interference hits only part of the band, an eavesdropper sees noise-like energy, and users share the band with different codes. GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and military links use it. Only a few universities teach this topic in depth.
prereq: You need Shannon capacity and S/N from 2.3, carrier modulation from 2.6, and band sharing from 2.7.

blocks.text: A narrowband signal is easy to jam: an interferer needs power only in that small band. Spread spectrum widens the signal on purpose using a code or hopping rule known to the receiver. The same watts now fill a wider band, so power per hertz falls; the signal may sit below the noise at any one frequency. The receiver correlates with the code and recovers the data. It also lets many users share one band with different codes, as in CDMA. Shannon capacity in 2.3 still limits the link; spreading changes the signal's shape, not the physics of noise.

sections.h3: Direct sequence: chips and processing gain

blocks.text: DSSS replaces each data bit with a chip sequence. A chip is one symbol of the spreading code, not a data bit. The code is a pseudo-random (PN) sequence known at both ends. The 11-chip Barker code is common; its autocorrelation peak is sharp. Chip rate exceeds bit rate, so bandwidth grows. The transmitter multiplies data by the PN code and modulates a carrier. The receiver multiplies by the same code, aligned in time, and integrates over one bit: wanted chips add coherently, while interference and other codes spread. Processing gain Gₚ compares chip rate R_chip to data rate R_data. In CDMA each user has a different PN code; a receiver treats other codes as noise (see Unit 3, Multiple access protocols).

blocks.where: Gₚ is processing gain in dB; R_chip is chip rate in chips per second; R_data is data rate in bits per second.

sections.h3: Frequency hopping: schedule and dwell time

blocks.text: FHSS moves the carrier among frequencies. The hop set is the list of allowed frequencies. One hop is one switch. Dwell time is the time on one frequency before the next hop. A pseudo-random schedule chooses the next frequency, so a jammer cannot predict it. In slow hopping, one hop carries several data bits. In fast hopping, several hops occur within one data bit, so the receiver must re-tune to the right frequency for every hop and combine several hops to recover one bit. Hop-set size does not set dwell time; hopping rate alone does: dwell time = 1 ÷ hops per second. Bluetooth Classic uses FHSS in the crowded 2.4 GHz band.

figure.caption: One data bit 1 is sent as the 11 chips of the Barker code; at the receiver the same code turns those chips into eleven +1s, which add to +11 and give back the bit, with processing gain 10.4 dB. A jammer's chips stay random after that same multiplication and add to about zero.

spec.title: 11 chips per bit, Gₚ = 10.4 dB
spec.aria: Rows show one data bit spread over 11 Barker chips, the received signal becoming eleven +1s that sum to +11 after multiplication by the same code, and jammer chips staying random and summing to about zero.

examples.question: A DSSS link sends data at 1 Mbit/s. An 11-chip Barker code gives 11 Mchip/s. (a) Find the processing gain in dB. (b) How much stronger must an interferer be to break the link? (c) An FHSS link has 50 hop frequencies and hops 200 times per second. Find the dwell time.
steps: Power ratio = 10^(10.414 ÷ 10) ≈ 11.0. Assuming the interferer's power lies inside the spread band, the receiver's processing gain of 11 (10.4 dB) suppresses it by that factor; it must be about 11 times stronger in power, within the spread band, to break the link.
Dwell = 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s = 5 ms; the 50 frequencies do not change it.
examples.answer: Processing gain is 10.4 dB; the interferer must be about 11 times stronger in power within the spread band; each hop lasts 5 ms.
examples.check:
import math
ratio = 11000000 / 1000000
pg = 10 * math.log10(ratio)
print(round(pg, 1))
print(round(10 ** (pg / 10), 0))
print(1 / 200 * 1000)

traps: Spreading raises bandwidth and lowers power per hertz, not total power or data rate.
Chip rate is not bit rate; chips per bit create processing gain, not user data.
Processing gain is a power ratio in dB: 10.4 dB means about 11 in power.
Fast hopping means several hops per data bit; slow hopping means several bits per hop.
Dwell time depends on hop rate, not the number of hop frequencies.

quiz.q: What is a chip in DSSS?
quiz.a: One symbol of the spreading code.

quiz.q: Why can a spread signal sit below the noise floor?
quiz.a: The receiver multiplies by the time-aligned code, so wanted chips add coherently and rebuild the bit, while noise and interference are spread over the wide band and only a small fraction of their power falls in the narrow data band; the resulting processing gain raises the signal-to-noise ratio by about Gₚ, so the received signal may be weaker than the noise in the wide band.

quiz.q: Data rate 2 Mbit/s, 11 chips per bit: find chip rate and processing gain.
An FHSS link hops 500 times per second. Find dwell time.
Interferer is 8 dB stronger; processing gain is 10.4 dB. Can the link work, and by what margin?
Why must the receiver's PN code be time-aligned?
quiz.a: Misalignment prevents coherent addition; the signal stays buried.

beyond: Not for exam. GPS uses DSSS so weak satellite signals are recovered below noise. Wi-Fi's older 802.11b mode used DSSS directly; newer Wi-Fi modes and 5G use OFDM with adaptive modulation and coding instead of spreading. 5G keeps frequency-hopping ideas mainly in frequency planning, not in the data waveform.
